strengths: Addresses a clearly motivated and practically important problem: constructing video detailed captioning (VDC) data without human annotations or larger teacher models, which meaningfully lowers the barrier relative to human-aligned (Cockatiel, ShareGPT4Video) and stronger-teacher (AVC-DPO, VideoCap-R1) pipelines.

The method is cleanly articulated and self-contained. The iterative loop (Eq. 1-3) is precisely formulated, the self-reflection trigger conditioned on score regression is a sensible design, and the curriculum DPO objective (Eq. 6) with easy-to-hard ordering by the score gap is a simple, well-justified use of an otherwise noisy signal.

Ablations are thorough and directly probe the claims: the decomposition of Principle vs. self-Reflection (Table 2) with inference-time accounting, curriculum DPO vs. vanilla DPO vs. SFT (Table 3), robustness of results to independently written principle sets P1-P3 (Table 4), and the effect of maximum iteration T with generation-time cost (Table 5).

Empirical results are consistent across all five VDC dimensions and support the central claim: VDC-Agent-7B reaches 49.08/2.50 average, surpassing caption-focused baselines at comparable scale and improving over the Qwen2.5-VL-7B base by +5.13 accuracy / +0.27 score.

Compute costs are reported transparently (Table 5 generation time, Table 2 inference time), and the paper correctly emphasizes that the fine-tuned model retains base-model inference cost, which is a genuine practical advantage over test-time self-reflection variants.
Writing is clear, the pipeline figure is informative, and the qualitative example (Fig. 3) illustrates reduced hallucination and richer grounding relative to baselines.
weaknesses: Novelty is moderate: agentic self-reflection, principle-guided self-scoring, and prompt refinement are largely adaptations of existing self-refinement / LLM-agent literature (Reflexion, ReAct) to the VDC data-construction setting, rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

The self-judging loop raises a circularity concern that is not addressed: the same base MLLM generates captions, assigns the 0-100 quality score, and produces suggestions, and this self-assigned score (with threshold λ=90) is the sole signal driving data selection and curriculum ordering. The reliability of this scorer is never validated against human judgment or an independent model, leaving open the risk that the loop reinforces the model's own stylistic biases rather than genuine caption quality.

The evaluation metric (VDCscore) is itself VLM-based, and the training preference signal is self-generated; there is potential coupling between the training objective and the evaluation criterion. Beyond a single hand-picked qualitative example, there is no independent faithfulness/hallucination evaluation or human study to confirm that the resulting captions are factually better.

Reported gains over the base model are modest (+5.13% accuracy, +0.27 score), and no variance, significance testing, or multi-seed results are provided, so the stability of the improvement is unclear.

The data-construction cost is substantial (e.g., 393.6h for T=4 in Table 5), yet the paper does not deeply analyze the trade-off between this upfront generation cost and the achieved gain, nor compare it against the cost of human annotation or teacher distillation it claims to replace.

There is limited discussion of limitations and failure modes—e.g., what happens when the self-scorer is systematically wrong, or when the model's initial prompt yields degenerate trajectories that survive filtering.

strengths: The problem is well-motivated and cleanly positioned: Figure 1 contrasts the three paradigms (human-aligned pipelines, stronger-teacher distillation, and the proposed agentic self-reflection), and the paper correctly identifies that prior VDC work depends either on proprietary/stronger teacher MLLMs (GPT-4V, Qwen2.5-72B in AVC-DPO) or extensive human annotation (Cockatiel, OwlCap). Removing both dependencies is a genuinely useful direction.

The agentic loop is well-specified rather than a vague 'LLM agent' wrapper: principle-guided scoring jointly emits a scalar score s_t and a natural-language suggestion g_t (Eq. 2), the prompt is refined accordingly, and a separate self-reflection branch is triggered specifically when s_t < s_{t-1} using the previous round's chain-of-thought to diagnose the failed update (Eq. 3). Distinguishing 'refine' from 'reflect' is a sensible design choice.

The most compelling practical insight is well supported by evidence: the benefit of test-time iterative reflection is distilled into a single forward pass via DPO. Table 2 quantifies this directly — Baseline+P+R reaches 47.10/2.38 at 164.9s inference time, while VDC-Agent reaches 49.08/2.50 at 15.5s, i.e. better quality at ~10x lower cost. This is a meaningful contribution beyond just 'use an LLM to self-improve'.

Curriculum DPO is simple, principled, and properly ablated. Exploiting the score gap Δs as a built-in easy-to-hard difficulty signal is a natural fit for the data the agent already produces, and Table 3 confirms the ordering SFT (47.54/2.41) < vanilla DPO (48.03/2.42) < Curriculum DPO (49.08/2.50).

The ablation suite is unusually thorough for this type of paper: robustness of the framework to the wording of principles using three independent contributors with different principle sets (Table 4, results stable around ~49.0/2.50), sensitivity to the maximum iteration T with generation-time accounting (Table 5), and a four-way comparison against naive principle injection and test-time reflection (Table 2).

The headline result is solid: 49.08 accuracy / 2.50 score on the VDC benchmark, best among all compared ~7B models, +5.13 acc / +0.27 score over the identical-backbone Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct baseline at the same inference cost, and above AVC-DPO (47.70/2.47) which requires a Qwen2.5-72B auxiliary model. Notably, VideoCap-R1-7B actually falls below the base model on accuracy, whereas VDC-Agent improves on it.

Reproducibility is reasonably good: public source corpora (Cockatiel-4K / OpenVid-1M), a public benchmark (VDC, 1,027 videos), explicit rule-based filtering (removal of trivial one-step cases and JSON-parsing errors), and complete training hyperparameters (LoRA rank 16 / alpha 32, dropout 0.1, 3 epochs, cosine schedule, LR 5e-5, 10% warmup, 4x A800, batch size 16).

The qualitative comparison in Fig. 3 is informative, with color coding that separates grounded descriptions from hallucinations and isolates fine-grained details captured only by VDC-Agent-7B, and it aligns with the quantitative trend.
weaknesses: The central scientific risk is not addressed: the scorer and the captioner share the same backbone and parameter set, and the self-assigned score is used simultaneously as (a) the reflection trigger, (b) the preference-pair selection criterion, (c) the curriculum difficulty signal, and (d) a reported metric proxy. No validation is provided that this score correlates with human judgment or with an independent judge. Without such a study, it is difficult to rule out that gains partly reflect the model learning to produce captions its own scorer prefers (self-consistency / reward-hacking bias) rather than genuinely better captions. This concern goes to the core claim of self-improvement without external supervision.

Evaluation is restricted to a single benchmark (VDC) and a single backbone (Qwen2.5-VL-7B). The introduction motivates VDC by its usefulness for video QA, text-to-video generation, and retrieval, but no downstream task evidence is given to show the improved captions transfer. Generality of the framework across backbones is deferred to future work, so the claim of a broadly applicable 'self-evolving framework' is only partially supported.

The paper contains no limitations or failure-mode discussion. In particular, the frequency with which the self-reflection branch actually triggers, and its contribution relative to plain prompt refinement during data generation, is never isolated. Table 2's 'Baseline+P+R' applies reflection at test time rather than ablating the reflection branch inside the training-data pipeline, so the specific value of the self-reflection mechanism (as opposed to iterative refinement alone) is not directly established.

Some design choices are left unjustified or un-ablated: the score threshold lambda = 90 (on a 0-100 scale) is never swept, and the relationship between the internal 0-100 score and the ~2.5 benchmark score reported in Table 1 is not explained, making the numbers harder to interpret.

The scale of the generated supervision is modest — 4,008 source videos yielding 20,040 raw trajectories and 18,886 retained pairs after discarding 1,078 trivial one-step samples and 76 malformed ones. It is also not stated whether VDC-Agent-19K will be publicly released, which limits the practical value of the 'annotation-free dataset' contribution.

The practical margin over the strongest competing specialized captioner is small (49.08 vs 47.70 accuracy, 2.50 vs 2.47 score against AVC-DPO), so the primary advantage is cost and annotation-freedom rather than a large quality jump; the paper would benefit from stating this trade-off more explicitly rather than emphasizing 'state-of-the-art' alone.

The prompt-update rule in Eq. 3 and the reflection trigger are heuristic (score-increase vs. score-decrease branches). This is acceptable for a systems contribution, but the paper presents it in a formalized way without discussing its brittleness — e.g., a single noisy score sample can flip the branch, and no variance/repeatability analysis of the scoring process is reported.

strengths: The paper frames the problem well: Figure 1 gives a clean taxonomy of video-captioning pipelines (human-aligned, stronger-teacher, and the proposed self-reflective agent), and the motivation—avoiding human annotation and proprietary/large teacher distillation—is clearly stated and practically relevant.

The method is described completely and reproducibly at the conceptual level: the agent loop (generation → principle-guided scoring → prompt refinement → self-reflection on regression) is formalized in Eqs. (1)–(3), the data construction into (x, y+, y−, Δs) tuples is spelled out, and Curriculum DPO is defined unambiguously.

The ablation suite is broader than typical for this venue: component ablation (Table 2), preference-optimization variants SFT vs. DPO vs. Curriculum DPO (Table 3), robustness to independently written principle sets by three contributors (Table 4), and an iteration-budget T study with generation-time accounting (Table 5).

A practically valuable property is demonstrated: because self-reflection is internalized during training, inference cost matches the base model (15.5s in Table 2), in contrast to test-time reflection, which inflates latency by ~10x.

The headline result is non-trivial in one respect: a 7B model trained only on self-generated data slightly exceeds AVC-DPO-7B (49.08/2.50 vs 47.70/2.47), a system that uses Qwen2.5-72B as a teacher, and improves over its own backbone by +5.13 Acc / +0.27 Score. The qualitative example in Fig. 3 is also reasonably convincing regarding hallucination reduction.
The paper is clearly written and well organized; the training/eval protocol (Cockatiel-4K videos only, no overlap with the VDC benchmark) is stated, which is a useful reproducibility signal.
weaknesses: The central supervision signal is never validated. The same backbone produces both the captions and the 0–100 quality scores (Eq. (2)), and these scores drive prompt refinement, the self-reflection trigger, best/worst selection, and the Δs curriculum. No calibration against human judgments, against VDCscore, or against any independent metric is reported. Since the very model shown in Fig. 3 to hallucinate (Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct) is also the scorer, the ability of that scorer to detect its own errors is an unverified assumption on which the entire contribution rests.

No analysis of reward hacking is provided. The target metric (VDCscore) is an LLM-judge-style measure that rewards detail/coverage, and the method optimizes captions toward high self-assigned detail scores. There is no reporting of caption length, hallucination rate, or factual-precision statistics for VDC-Agent-7B vs. baselines, so the reported +5.13 Acc could partly reflect stylistic drift toward verbose, detail-dense outputs rather than genuine grounding.

The comparison against prior methods is confounded. Baselines such as ShareGPT4Video-8B, Vriptor, AuroraCap, Cockatiel-8B and VideoCap-R1-7B are built on different (often older) backbones and different training corpora; the only controlled comparison is against Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct itself. Decomposing the gain via Table 3, plain SFT on the self-generated data already yields 47.54 (+3.59 over the 43.95 baseline), while the proposed agentic + curriculum machinery adds only ~+1.5. The paper does not isolate how much of the final number comes from the claimed self-reflection mechanism versus generic task-specific fine-tuning on Cockatiel-domain video.

Statistical strength of the gains is unclear. Several dimension-level differences are within rounding (camera 50.52/2.67 vs AVC-DPO 50.40/2.66; short 39.49 vs 37.76), the average advantage over the strongest baseline is ~1.4 Acc points, and no seed variance, confidence intervals, or repeated-run statistics are reported. Single-benchmark (VDC) evidence alone is thin for the claim of 'state of the art' and 'stronger captioner'.

Novelty and attribution are under-developed. Iterative generation of preference pairs from a model's own judgments followed by DPO (self-rewarding language models), principle/constitution-based self-critique, and curriculum/easy-to-hard preference learning are all established ideas; the paper cites Reflexion and ReAct but does not engage with self-rewarding LM literature or LLM-as-judge calibration work, and therefore does not establish what is new beyond the video-domain application and the Δs-based sampler.

The efficiency framing is partially misleading. While no larger teacher is used at inference, constructing VDC-Agent-19K requires ~70.7s per video and ~393.6 A800-GPU-hours at T=4 (Table 5). This cost is not discussed against the 'no external models / low cost' motivation. Similarly, 'requires neither human annotations' overstates the setting: the principles are human-authored, the five task dimensions are human-designed, and the video source is a curated high-resolution subset, so scalability to genuinely arbitrary unlabeled video is not demonstrated.

Evaluation is limited to one benchmark with no downstream validation. Claims that VDC-Agent-7B is a 'stronger video detailed captioner' would be much better supported by transfer results (video QA, retrieval, temporal grounding) or a human preference study; neither is provided. Additionally, reliance on Cockatiel-4K videos (which were originally paired with GPT-4o-generated captions) deserves a clearer discussion of how much of the domain prior is inherited from that corpus.

strengths: Proposes VDC-Agent, an autonomous self-evolving framework for video detailed captioning that eliminates per-video human annotations and external teacher MLLMs by using principle-guided iterative self-reflection.

Introduces the VDC-Agent-19K preference dataset and a curriculum DPO strategy that uses the score gap between preferred and dispreferred captions as a difficulty signal, with ablations showing easy-to-hard ordering outperforms random and anti-curriculum variants.

Achieves state-of-the-art results on VDC and DREAM-1K benchmarks, with consistent improvements across three base MLLMs (LLaVA-OneVision, InternVL2.5, Qwen2.5-VL), demonstrating cross-model generalization.
Provides extensive empirical validation, including human preference evaluation, GPT-5.1 judge evaluation, ablations on principles, maximum iteration T, and a compute-normalized Best-of-N comparison.
The paper is clearly written and well organized, with informative figures and tables that make the proposed pipeline and experimental setup easy to follow.
weaknesses: The preference data is generated from the same model's self-assigned scores, so the training signal may inherit self-evaluation biases; human agreement with the selected preferred captions is only 67.6–75.8%, which is not overwhelming.

The improvement of curriculum DPO over random DPO is modest (e.g., 49.08 vs. 48.03 average accuracy on VDC), and no variance or statistical significance is reported, so the claim that curriculum ordering is essential may be somewhat overstated.

Reproducibility is limited: no code or project page is provided, and several important details (principles, prompts, pseudo-code, dataset filtering specifics) are deferred to an appendix that is not available in the supplied manuscript.

The length-bias analysis appears inconsistent: the text states that y+ is moderately longer on average, but Fig. 3 seems to show y+ with a shorter average length than y-, which should be clarified or corrected.
The framework still relies on human-authored textual principles, even though robustness to different principles is ablated; a limitations discussion and broader societal-impact discussion are absent.

strengths: The paper addresses a well-motivated problem in video detailed captioning: eliminating dependence on expensive human annotations and larger proprietary teacher models. The paradigm comparison in Fig. 1 (human-aligned vs. stronger-teacher vs. agentic self-reflection) is clear and effectively positions the contribution.

The proposed VDC-Agent framework is coherent and well designed: principle-guided evaluation, a decision node that distinguishes prompt refinement from self-reflection triggered by score degradation, and chain-of-thought-based error diagnosis form a sensible closed loop. The formalization (Eqs. 1-3) is clean and readable.

Internalizing the iterative self-reflection into the model via DPO is a practically valuable contribution. Table 4 convincingly shows that test-time reflection (Baseline+P+R) yields only modest gains at prohibitive inference cost (164.9s), whereas the internalized VDC-Agent matches or exceeds it at base-model latency (15.5s). This is a meaningful efficiency/performance result.

The Curriculum DPO idea—using the score gap Δs as a built-in difficulty signal for easy-to-hard ordering—is simple but effective, and is properly validated. Table 5 shows the curriculum ordering outperforms random and anti-curriculum DPO, and the ablation is well controlled.

Empirical evidence is broad and convincing. SOTA on VDC (49.08% avg acc, 2.50 score), consistent gains on DREAM-1K F1/Precision/Recall, and, importantly, method-agnostic transfer to three distinct base models (LLaVA-OneVision-7B, InternVL2.5-8B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B). The improvements on fine-grained dimensions (camera, background, main object) over the 'Short' dimension are consistent with the stated goal.

The paper preempts several obvious reviewer concerns: (a) the length-bias analysis in Fig. 3 with overlapping distributions plus human preference evaluation (Tab. 3) argues that preference is not merely driven by length; (b) the robustness-to-principles study across P1-P4 (Tab. 6) shows results are not sensitive to exact principle wording; (c) the compute-normalized Best-of-N comparison (Tab. 8) argues the gains come from directed reasoning rather than extra test-time compute; (d) the maximum-iteration ablation (Tab. 7) characterizes the performance/latency trade-off.

The human pairwise preference study (Tab. 3, 67.6-75.8% agreement with the agent's scores) is a reasonable attempt to validate that the self-assigned scores reflect human notions of quality. Training videos come from Cockatiel-4K/OpenVid-1M with an explicit statement of no overlap with evaluation benchmarks, and the qualitative example in Fig. 4 shows genuinely more grounded, less hallucinated captions.
The writing is clear and the paper is well organized; the method section is easy to follow despite several details being deferred to the appendix.
weaknesses: The most substantive scientific concern is that the same MLLM backbone is used both as caption generator and as the principle-guided critic/scorer (Eq. 2). The paper does not directly validate the calibration or reliability of this self-scorer (e.g., correlation of s_t with human ratings at the per-caption level), only indirectly via top-vs-bottom pairwise preference (Tab. 3). It remains possible that the curriculum DPO partly learns to satisfy the model's own scoring idiosyncrasies rather than a purely external notion of caption quality. The consistent DREAM-1K and human-evaluation gains mitigate this, but a more direct analysis of scorer reliability would substantially strengthen the claim.

Novelty is somewhat incremental: self-reflection, self-scoring, and DPO for captioning are all established components. The core novelty is their combination plus the curriculum-DPO scheduling. The paper would benefit from a clearer discussion of how it differs from closely related self-rewarding/self-refine/AVC-DPO lines beyond the paradigm figure.

Several important details are deferred to the appendix (principles R, pseudo-code, self-reflection trigger rate, system prompts), making it difficult to fully assess reproducibility from the main text alone. The self-reflection trigger rate in particular is relevant to understanding how often the additional reasoning path is exercised.

The rule-based filtering that discards samples already reaching the threshold λ in the first iteration (1,078 pairs removed) could bias the preference data toward harder cases and is not ablated; it is unclear whether this filtering materially affects final performance.

The claim of 'state-of-the-art' is largely benchmark-specific (VDCscore and DREAM-1K). Given that the metric is itself a learned/criteria-based score, stronger evidence would come from showing the gains hold on an independent, human-annotated captioning benchmark not derived from the same evaluation family.

The paper offers only a brief future-work statement and little explicit discussion of limitations (e.g., reliance on a single high-resolution source corpus Cockatiel-4K, sensitivity to the base model's scoring ability, potential failure modes when the base model's critique is wrong). A limitations/societal-impact discussion would strengthen the submission.

The compute cost of dataset construction (T=4 iterations × 5 dimensions over 4,008 videos) is non-trivial; while the paper reports generation times in Tab. 7, a clearer accounting of the total offline data-generation cost relative to the distillation-based baselines would be informative.

strengths: Clear, well-structured presentation: the self-reflection loop, dataset construction and curriculum DPO are described with a readable figure (Fig. 2) and equations, and the experimental setup (LoRA rank/alpha, LR, batch size, T=4, λ=90, decoding parameters) is specified in enough detail to be reproduced.

The gains are consistent across three different backbones (LLaVA-OneVision-7B, InternVL2.5-8B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B) and on two benchmarks, which is more than a single-model result and supports the claim of method-agnostic applicability of the framework.

DREAM-1K results provide some independent (non-self-scored) evidence: F1 improves by +5.2 to +7.3 with event-level precision/recall against human annotations, which is harder to explain away as pure verbosity than the VDCscore numbers alone.

The ablation suite is unusually broad for this kind of paper: component ablation (Table 4), curriculum ordering including anti-curriculum (Table 5), robustness to four independently written principle sets including industry guidelines (Table 6), iteration budget T (Table 7), and a compute-normalized Best-of-N comparison (Table 8).

A genuine practical advantage is demonstrated: internalization keeps inference latency at base-model level (15.5s) versus test-time reflection (164.9s), while still outperforming it, which is a relevant deployment argument.
The motivation (avoiding GPT-4V distillation and expensive human annotation for VDC training data) is legitimate and timely, and the qualitative example in Fig. 4 is illustrative.
weaknesses: The central premise is unvalidated: the whole data pipeline (scores s_t, preference pairs, difficulty signal Δs) rests on the base MLLM scoring its own outputs, and the paper provides no analysis of the evaluator's reliability (calibration, repeatability, position/verbosity bias, agreement with humans on arbitrary pairs rather than max-vs-min pairs). The only check (Table 3) shows humans prefer the self-designated y+ in just 67.6–75.8% of cases, i.e., a substantial fraction of the DPO training pairs are noisy or inverted, and Δs — the quantity curriculum DPO sorts on — is therefore of questionable validity. This is a consequential gap for a paper whose headline claim is autonomous self-evaluation without external supervision.

The human study does not validate the actual contribution. Table 3 only audits preference pairs inside VDC-Agent-19K; there is no human comparison of VDC-Agent captions against baselines, so the abstract's claim of validation 'by both quantitative metrics and human evaluation' overstates the evidence. It is also not stated whether annotators had access to the videos (essential for judging hallucination/faithfulness), nor is inter-annotator agreement or annotator qualification reported, and the large gap between human (~70%) and GPT-5.1 (~90%) preference rates is left unexplained.

The marginal contribution of the elaborate agentic machinery is small and not isolated. Simply concatenating the principles into the prompt (Baseline+P) already gives 46.47 vs 43.95 for the baseline; the full pipeline reaches 49.08, so roughly half the total gain comes from a trivial prompt change. There is no ablation in which preference pairs are built without self-reflection (e.g., Best-of-N captions scored by the same evaluator, or pairs from the base model's own sampling), so it is not established that agentic self-reflection, rather than ordinary self-training/self-rewarding on self-generated data, is responsible for the remaining gain.

Possible verbosity confound is asserted away rather than tested. y+ is longer than y- (Fig. 3) and VDCscore rewards detail, yet no length-controlled experiment (fixed output length, length-penalized metric, or matched-length comparison) is provided; the claim that preference is 'largely attributable to content quality rather than length alone' is not demonstrated. This also complicates the interpretation of the 'Short' dimension, where gains are smallest.

Key experimental details and rigor are missing: the 'VDC-Agent (SFT)' row in Table 5 does not specify the training data or objective, so the DPO gain cannot be fully attributed; no multiple seeds, variance, or significance tests are reported, so differences such as 48.03 vs 49.08 (random vs curriculum DPO) or 49.08 vs 47.70 (vs AVC-DPO) are not shown to exceed run-to-run noise; baseline decoding settings are not stated to match the proposed model's (beam 1, temperature 0.1, max length 1024).

Novelty is incremental and the closest prior art is not confronted. Self-critique-based refinement (Self-Refine), self-generated preference data (self-rewarding/self-instruct style), DPO, and curriculum ordering are all established components; 'curriculum DPO' here amounts to re-sorting the same DPO loss by Δs with no analysis beyond intuition, and no comparison against related self-training/self-rewarding baselines is given. The claim of 'no external supervision' is also softer than presented: human-written principles, a hand-designed initial prompt, and a strong base MLLM are all required.

Evaluation circularity is not discussed: VDCscore and the GPT-5.1 preference judge are themselves MLLM-based, so gains measured by an LLM judge on an LLM-centric pipeline share potential biases (length, fluency, detail) with the training signal; the paper should at least acknowledge and, ideally, control for this.

Reproducibility and attribution: the project page is empty, no code/data release statement is given, the dataset construction and prompt details are repeatedly deferred to an appendix, and the reference list contains a large cluster of citations to a small set of authors on topics largely unrelated to video captioning (incremental learning, domain adaptation, segmentation), which reads as citation padding.

Minor technical sloppiness: in Eq. (3) the prompt-refinement branch does not actually include the suggestion g_t even though the text says the update uses it, and the piecewise rule omits several boundary cases; the 'Human/External' annotation of the improved rows in Table 1 is also confusing.
